# Greek letters {#sec-greek}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
The one like the fish.
:::

Once, a colleague gave a lecture on Lotka-Volterra equation to undergraduate students in the biology department. When a student asked: "what is alpha?", she spent a few minutes explaining what alpha represented until another student interjected and said: "it is the one like the fish". That was an unexpected knowledge gap, but also more common that not.

Many should remember the "identité remarquable" $(a + b) ^ 2 = a^2 + b^2 + 2ab$, but bamboozled with $(\zeta  + \xi)^2 = \zeta^2 + \xi^2 + 2\zeta\xi$. Yet, it is the same identity. Likewise, calculting $13 + 9 = 22$ is trivial, but it requires a certain amount of brainpower to calculate $XIII + IX$ (the answer is $XXII$).

Many are comfortable to perform calculation with the Hindu-Arabic numerals, not with roman number. Yet, equally comfortable using roman numerals when refering to sections in the bible. The roman indicate one is talking about the seciont while romans are reserved for the verses.^[Could you imagine how cumbersome if it was the opposite!]

So what is the need of greek letter? It is not really needed, but it is convenient in the right context.

## Formal {.unnumbered}

Here is dictionary of the greek alphabet in upper and lower case, the latin equivalent, and how to call them

| Lower Case | Upper Case | Latin Equivalent | Name    |
|:-----------|:-----------|:-----------------|:--------|
| $\alpha$   | $A$        | a                | Alpha   |
| $\beta$    | $B$        | b                | Beta    |
| $\gamma$   | $\Gamma$   | g                | Gamma   |
| $\delta$   | $\Delta$   | d                | Delta   |
| $\epsilon$ | $E$        | e                | Epsilon |
| $\zeta$    | $Z$        | z                | Zeta    |
| $\eta$     | $H$        | e                | Eta     |
| $\theta$   | $\Theta$   | th               | Theta   |
| $\iota$    | $I$        | i                | Iota    |
| $\kappa$   | $K$        | k                | Kappa   |
| $\lambda$  | $\Lambda$  | l                | Lambda  |
| $\mu$      | $M$        | m                | Mu      |
| $\nu$      | $N$        | n                | Nu      |
| $\xi$      | $\Xi$      | x                | Xi      |
| $\omicron$ | $O$        | o                | Omicron |
| $\pi$      | $\Pi$      | p                | Pi      |
| $\rho$     | $R$        | r                | Rho     |
| $\sigma$   | $\Sigma$   | s                | Sigma   |
| $\tau$     | $T$        | t                | Tau     |
| $\upsilon$ | $\Upsilon$ | y                | Upsilon |
| $\phi$     | $\Phi$     | ph               | Phi     |
| $\chi$     | $X$        | ch               | Chi     |
| $\psi$     | $\Psi$     | ps               | Psi     |
| $\omega$   | $\Omega$   | o                | Omega   |


## Examples {.unnumbered}

* "I am $\alpha$ and $\Omega$": probably the most famous use of Greek letters to mean the beginning and the end.
* $\pi$ represents the number $3.14\dots$ and geometrically is the ratio between the circumference of a circle and its diameter.
* $\sigma$ denotes standard deviation, while variance is $\sigma^2$.
* $\sum$ and $\prod$ represent summation and product, respectively (see @sec-sum).
* The Riemann zeta function $\zeta(s)$ is an important function; a conjectured property called the Riemann hypothesis has remained unproven so far.
* $\epsilon$, $\omicron$, and $\iota$ were used to designate COVID-19 variants.

## Tips and warning {.unnumbered}

* In mathematics, Greek letters often represent parameters while Latin letters represent variables, for example $x(t) = \alpha t^2 + \beta$.
* In probability and statistics, Greek letters represent parameters of a probability distribution: $\mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma)$ or $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$.
* $\alpha$ is used as a threshold in statistical significance, $\beta$ for Type II error, and $\varepsilon$ or $\epsilon$^[The curly and lunate forms are two typographic styles for epsilon due to historical conventions.] represents a random error.
* In statistics, Greek letters denote the true population value—for instance, $\sigma$ for the standard deviation of the population (@sec-population)—and $s$ or $\hat{\sigma}$ for the estimated value from the sample. This will become clearer when statistical inference is addressed.^[Not yet in this version.]
